title: The East, again
tomorrow: what was a brilliant young man in Milan so restless for?

cards: Swimmers learn to breathe on both sides. Breathe only to one side and you can still swim, but you drift, and you tire sooner. Pope John Paul the Second used a picture like that for the whole Church.
In a letter on Christian unity, he wrote that the Church must breathe with her two lungs, the East and the West. So what is the other lung, and what does it breathe?

teach.b: The question is: can Christians who pray so differently still belong to one body? The East is the Christianity of Greece, the Middle East, Russia, Ukraine, Egypt, Ethiopia, India and more.
Some Eastern Churches are Catholic, in full communion with the pope, with their own liturgies and saints.
Here's the one to tell a friend: in Eastern Catholic Churches, married men can be ordained priests, by their own tradition. And then there's the neighbor: the Orthodox Churches.

teach.h: THE ORTHODOX: LOVE, THEN THE CREED.
teach.b: In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, just before the Creed, the deacon calls out, in effect: let us love one another, that with one mind we may confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Love first, then the Creed.
Catholics recognize so much shared ground: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, Mary honored as Theotokos, the God-bearer, and icons.
A council at Nicaea taught that the honor given an icon passes to the one it shows. The difference is honest, too. Catholics and Orthodox aren't in full communion.
Orthodox Christians don't accept the pope's authority as Catholics understand it, and that difference is real.
Jesus prayed in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Not the same. Not strangers.
Two lungs that have learned to breathe in different rhythms.

how: Eastern Catholic Churches celebrate their own liturgies, like the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, in full communion with the pope; Catholics and Orthodox Christians both pray with icons and honor Mary as Theotokos, while working through what still divides them.

games.q: your Orthodox friend asks if your churches are basically the same now. what's the fairest answer?
o: close kin: shared sacraments, Mary, icons; not yet one communion, mainly over the pope.
yes, exactly the same; only the language and music are different.
no real connection; the two split apart long ago and share nothing now.
games.why: the shared ground is deep, and the difference is honest. John Paul II's picture: one body that must breathe with both lungs.

practice: Find an icon or a holy image, on a wall or a screen; if there isn't one, a photo of someone you love will do. Look at the face, especially the eyes, and breathe slowly, both sides of your chest filling.
If you pray, you can pray with the image as Eastern Christians do, letting the honor pass through it to the one it shows.

wordCard.voice: The East. The Christian traditions of the East, Catholic and Orthodox: one of the Church's two lungs.

orig.note: Greek: God-bearer. the title for Mary honored by Catholics and Orthodox alike.

carryVoice: Keep this: both lungs, East and West, not the same and not strangers. That's today.
